newsitem.title: FIJI: FEATURE - Fiji horse races test both man and beast.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fiji horse races test both man and beast.

text.p: The Fiji Charity Horse Races are not for the faint-hearted.
The horses, cantankerous beasts hauled off the sugar cane farms and tobacco plantations scattered around the island of Viti Levu, are more inclined to kick and bite than race.

The jockeys are tough, leathery men who don't mind a few bruises or a broken limb. The few boys that saddle up are simply too young to realise the dangers, but fortunately seem to have glue on their backsides.

The spectators, a mixture of local Fijians and expatriates, are hardy as well, coping with the blazing South Pacific sun by consuming enough beer or Kava, a local intoxicant, to flood the dusty racetrack.
But it's all for a good cause. Proceeds from the bi-annual event go to charity. A recent meeting raised F$7,500 (US$5,850) for a hospital for mentally-handicapped children.

The 800-metre long oval racetrack of the Votualevu Fields is down a rock-strewn dirt road that meanders through tobacco farms behind the town of Nadi on the west coast of the main island of Viti Levu. The track circles a plot of tobacco plants on the edge of the Nadi River, separated by a railing of white-washed bamboo.
For those who don't wish to pay F$5 for seats in the thatched-roof wooden grandstand, F$2 will get you plank seating up a hill under a tree.

There are no bookmakers and no odds are given. Bets are placed at a stall equipped with a totalisator machine, which divides winnings among punters according to the size of their bet, but only after 40 percent of the money wagered is taken out for charity. But even the smallest win sparks cries of joy from the punters.
Beer is sold from a caged stall under the watchful eye of a burly beer tent security officer.

On arrival, the first race has just been run and it has not been a good start. There's been a pile-up of horses and jockeys in the "Childrens' Race" for boy jockeys, although no one is hurt. Entry fee for the race was F$1, with a first prize of F$25.
A glance at the shoes of one jockey in the second race indentifies him as the favourite. Most riders are barefoot, gripping their stirrups between their toes. A few choose football socks.
But Abdul Asahim, a stick-thin Indian-Fijian, is equipped with black and red plastic hunting boots that zip up the back. He easily wins and goes on to be named jockey of the meet.
Race four is one of the big highlights, the 1,200-metre Rough Riders Race for local horses, no saddles or bridles.

The starter drops his flag and jockeys scramble to mount their bolting steeds in a start reminiscent of the Le Mans auto race, where drivers race to their cars before jumping in and zooming off. In the melee, one jockey is dragged by his heels, clutching his horse's mane. He finally drops to the ground, only to be kicked by another horse. As the dust settles, he limps off the track, but will return.
The end of each race sees the grandstand choking in dust and a rush to the bar for another beer or two and another coconut shell filled with Kava for the stewards.
Race five sees a blonde, pony-tailed jockey set the grandstand abuzz. Susan Snijdeis, from Eindhoven in Holland, has been in Fiji on a one-year holiday and has become a local favourite at the races.

"I can't believe I won. I didn't know where to pass, it's so dangerous. I was so afraid I would fall off," says Snijdeis, whose equestrian skills were limited to the more genteel dressage and show-jumping before she came to Fiji.

In race eight, the feature race, the Rothmans Trophy is at stake and the handlers of defending champion Trigger are pampering their entrant. Shaded by a tarpaulin before the race, Trigger has spent the day with his head on a pillow, as his trainer gently pats him. It proves a winning formula.
In the later races the meet's wilder side emerges.

Race nine is a chariot-style race aboard local sleds normally used to haul fertiliser on sugar and tobacco farms. It makes the savage chariot race in the film "Ben Hur" look like a trot around the park.
In the day's final race, the 1,400-metre Cross Country event, jockeys and horses charge out of the trees, across the brown Nadi River and back around the track.
By the end of the day, both men and beasts are bruised and battered, but there are no injuries, except for tomorrow's hangovers.
"It's a little different from Ascot...but it's a hell of a lot of fun," says race announcer Andrew Thomson, a local hotelier and scuba diving operator.
